abstract: Trait loss and genome size reduction are classic evolutionary signatures of obligate bacterial endosymbiosis. However, many bacteria are facultative endosymbionts and so experience a trade-off between adaptation to living within their hosts and apart from them. A central tension in this transition is whether traits required for independent life, including adaptations for interspecific competition, are maintained or lost. We compared three facultatively endosymbiotic Paraburkholderia species associated with the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum to test whether host adaptation is associated with reduced competitive ability. Two species, P. bonniea and P. hayleyella, display relatively small, streamlined genomes, while the other, P. agricolaris, has an unreduced genome compared to free-living congeners. We competed these species and three non-amoeba-associated Paraburkholderia against six ecologically relevant competitor bacteria, using fluorescent markers to track strain-specific fitness in co-culture. The reduced-genome species were never more competitive than P. agricolaris and, unlike P. agricolaris, never outcompeted their competitors. This deficit was reflected in a reduced ability to grow quickly to high levels in co-culture. Follow-up assays revealed that cell-free supernatant from the co-culture of P. agricolaris and a Pseudomonas isolate inhibited subsequent growth of the Pseudomonas, whereas supernatant from the co-culture of P. hayleyella and Pseudomonas did not. Reduced genome size in these facultative endosymbionts is associated with weaker competitive performance without eliminating independent proliferation under laboratory conditions. This competitive erosion may lead to ecological host dependence, where symbionts remain physiologically capable of living independently but become increasingly unable to persist outside the host in competitive microbial communities.
